analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run "Medicare Part E" health plan anyone can buy, and expands ACA subsidies.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since its June 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The Choose Medicare Act would create a public health insurance option — "Medicare Part E" — that any U.S. resident could buy on the insurance exchanges, that employers could voluntarily offer workers, and that would cover gold-level benefits including abortion care regardless of state bans [S2]. It would also cap out-of-pocket costs in traditional Medicare at $6,700 a year, make ACA premium subsidies more generous and lift the income cap on them, add a $30 billion reinsurance fund to lower marketplace costs, and let Medicare's drug-price negotiation apply to the new public plans [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured people gain a public plan alternative to private insurance, with richer subsidies and cost-sharing help for ACA marketplace enrollees. Workers with unaffordable employer coverage gain a voluntary employer option that they can keep even after losing a job. Traditional Medicare beneficiaries gain a first-time $6,700 annual out-of-pocket cap [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public plans that any U.S. resident not already on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP can buy on the exchanges, offered at gold-level coverage including abortion and reproductive care that state bans cannot block [S2].
Lets any employer voluntarily offer Part E to workers, with the government acting as plan administrator and letting workers keep the plan if they lose their job [S2].

Imposes a $6,700 annual out-of-pocket cap on people in traditional Medicare (starting in 2027, indexed to medical inflation) — traditional Medicare currently has no limit on how much a beneficiary can be made to pay in a year [S2].

Strengthens ACA marketplace help: premium subsidies would be benchmarked to gold plans instead of silver, the 400%-of-poverty income cap on subsidies would be removed, cost-sharing reductions would be richer, and a $30 billion reinsurance and affordability fund would lower individual-market costs in 2026–2028 [S2].

Uses Medicare's pricing power: Part E pays providers no more, in aggregate, than average exchange rates and applies Medicare's negotiated drug prices — with an excise-tax penalty on drug makers that refuse to comply — and bars participating providers from balance billing patients [S2].

Extends fair-rating rules (no charging more for pre-existing conditions) to the large-employer market and strengthens federal and state review of excessive or unjustified rates, including for grandfathered plans [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers would lose customers to a cheaper public competitor; hospitals and other providers would face payment rates capped below what commercial insurers typically pay, with mandatory participation and no balance billing; drug makers would face Medicare-negotiated prices in a new market; taxpayers would fund $2 billion in startup costs, $30 billion in reinsurance, and the expanded, uncapped subsidies — the bill includes no revenue offsets [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, hospitals, drug makers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill costs real money with no way to pay for it: $2 billion in startup funding, $30 billion for reinsurance, and permanently expanded subsidies with the income cap removed — the added federal cost is not offset by any tax or savings [S2].

Every Medicare-participating provider is automatically forced into the Part E network at rates capped below average commercial rates, which would cut hospital and physician revenue and limits their ability to negotiate — the bill bets this will not shrink access to care [S2].

Part E premiums must fully finance the plan's own costs, so savings for consumers depend on the public plan actually operating more cheaply than private plans; the bill guarantees the option, not the price advantage [S2].

A public option leaves private insurers in place and does not cap what they can charge outside the plan, so it does less for affordability than a single-payer system would — a limit its own supporters acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage and affordability gains are large and broad: a public option open to nearly everyone, a first-ever out-of-pocket cap for traditional Medicare, and noticeably richer marketplace help. The honest costs are also real — an unoffset multi-year federal commitment on top of the $32 billion explicitly appropriated, and payment cuts imposed on hospitals and doctors who have no choice about participating. This is the most ambitious version of a public option that still preserves private insurance, and its fiscal design (all benefits, no offsets) is the kind that makes passage unlikely in a cost-conscious Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has had no hearing, markup, or vote so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Choose Medicare Act in the Senate on June 11, 2025, joined by 10 Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day; that referral is the last action in the record [S4].
Eleven Senate Democrats had signed on as cosponsors, all from the Democratic caucus; no Republican has [S3].
The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive, but it has sat untouched in committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers are better off so far, because a public competitor with Medicare-based prices has not advanced; the current private system continues unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

sides.party_line_note: There has been no vote, but all 12 sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, while the Republican Senate majority controls the committee that would move the bill.

industries.note: Part E would compete with private plans in every market using cheaper government payment rates, taking insurers' customers; but the bill also hands insurers a $30 billion reinsurance fund and steers more generously subsidized customers to marketplace plans. Insurers have historically opposed public options because a cheaper public alternative threatens their core business.

Part E provider rates are capped, in aggregate, below average commercial rates, participation is automatic for Medicare providers, and balance billing is barred — all cutting revenue. In exchange, providers get guaranteed patient volume with no network negotiation.

The bill applies Medicare's negotiated drug prices to Part E plans and extends an excise-tax penalty to drug makers that do not negotiate, opening a large new market where government-set prices apply.

Employers could voluntarily shift workers to a Part E plan at premium rates set below average commercial rates, though employers without affordable plans must refer full-time workers to ACA navigators.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and chairing the Finance Committee, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a vote. The realistic path is that it sits in committee and expires with the 119th Congress on January 3, 2027, as most public-option proposals have in past Congresses.
